implementation_notes: Mutex#synchronize is the block-scoped guard: it acquires the mutex, yields the block and releases in an ensure clause, so the lock is freed on normal return, break, throw and exceptions. Ruby's Monitor (and MonitorMixin::ConditionVariable) provides the reentrant variant with the same block shape, and concurrent-ruby's ReadWriteLock applies it to reader/writer semantics. The classic hand-written guard is unnecessary; use synchronize, and only reach for Monitor when intra-object calls genuinely re-acquire the lock.
pitfalls: Mutex#synchronize is not reentrant: calling another synchronized method from inside the block raises ThreadError (deadlock; recursive locking) - restructure or use Monitor.
A Mutex is process-local; coordinating across processes needs file locks, a database lock or Redis, not Ruby's Mutex.
Blocking work inside synchronize (I/O, sleep, HTTP) holds the lock for the whole block and serializes all callers.
Ruby's GVL does not protect multi-step state transitions: synchronize is still required for check-then-act on shared state.
